Foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding. President George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that “foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.” The old methods have certainly not gone out of vogue; just this week Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. But today, a new type of foreign agent has arrived: Chinese artificial intelligence companies.
Like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use. But their makers train them to promote the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). American businesses are outsourcing more and more critical decisions to AI. If Washington does nothing, those businesses will hand over control to models whose objective is to promote a foreign government.
Although U.S. policymakers now debate banning Chinese AI, the tried-and-true American solution is not censorship but disclosure. In 1938, Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Rather than outlaw propaganda, FARA allowed foreign agents to continue spreading it—as long as they registered with the government and disclosed whom they really worked for. Their communications also had to carry a conspicuous label naming their foreign sponsor.
FARA’s wisdom has aged well over the decades. In recent years, the Justice Department has ordered the Russian state television network RT and the Chinese state media organizations Xinhua and CGTN to register as foreign agents and to label their content as such. Those who failed to register as foreign agents, such as Paul Manafort, President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign chairman, and former U.S. Representative David Rivera of Florida, were sentenced to prison. (Trump pardoned Manafort in 2020.)
Today, rather than banning AI companies controlled by foreign governments, the United States should treat them as foreign agents under FARA. No new statute is needed. Washington should simply enforce the one on the books. Of course, FARA is no silver bullet against all foreign influence, but it fits the shape of this problem. A handful of known Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, build the models that American businesses increasingly let think and act for them. The Justice Department can reach every one of them.
Democracy is strong enough to survive foreign influence but not invisible foreign influence. And to make sure the world does not subordinate its decision-making to Beijing, Washington and its allies must create an allied AI compact and then spread their own models far and wide.
American AI models, such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, are under no obligation to promote the U.S. government’s message. Ask Claude about Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s biggest failures or about the United States’ darkest chapters, and it will answer. Not so for Chinese AI models. When I asked the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek to “tell me about the CCP” in November, it answered that the party “is the vanguard of the Chinese working class, the Chinese people, and the Chinese nation. . . . The Party’s leadership is the most essential characteristic of socialism with Chinese characteristics and is the fundamental guarantee for China’s development and progress.” Such boosterish language appears by design.
By law, Chinese AI models must never go against the Chinese government. Under the country’s 2023 regulations on generative AI, they must “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and may not engage in “harming the nation’s image” or “undermining national unity and social stability.” The Chinese government released a technical standard that laid out what these high-level declarations mean in practice: AI developers should have a list of at least 10,000 banned keywords, and their models must refuse to answer at least 95 percent of test questions the CCP finds objectionable. Developers must also scrub their training data of any history Beijing does not like. In short, the models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.
That is why, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s AI evaluators found in 2025, DeepSeek pushes Chinese propaganda at far higher rates than American models do, even when run on American servers. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service found that DeepSeek inserted praise of the Chinese state unprompted, and it concluded that China uses DeepSeek to instill “a distorted, self-serving world view in the Western information space.”
Chinese AI models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.
But these models are not just propaganda parrots—they are taught to “think” about how to promote Beijing’s perspective. Ask an AI model something complex, and it will “reason” for a while. As it thinks, it produces an internal monologue called its chain of thought. Users rarely see it. There, it decides which facts are relevant and which to discard, what advice to give, and what autonomous actions to take. Silicon Valley is terrified that these chains of thought will become corrupt—that models will start scheming and lying, becoming “misaligned.” But a different kind of corruption is already here.
Although American models’ chains of thought usually focus on helping the user, China’s do something else: prioritize the party line. When researchers funded by Sweden’s Psychological Defense Agency looked at how Qwen, Alibaba’s flagship model, reasons about China, they found an internal checklist to keep the answer positive, avoid criticism, and focus on achievements. So when an American company asks a question on which Beijing has a view, a Chinese model may discard all evidence that points the other way. As the world delegates more research, writing, and decision-making to Chinese AI models, it risks infusing the CCP’s goals into every action taken.
These models are also highly persuasive. In a study published last year in Nature, researchers had some 6,000 voters in the United States, Canada, and Poland chat with AI models that argued for a candidate. The study found that a single conversation shifted the preferences of opposition voters in Canada and Poland by about ten percentage points. AI persuades by flooding a user with confident and authoritative-sounding facts—statistics, historical claims, and the like.
Chinese AI models also exhibit strange behaviors beyond the spreading of propaganda. In October, the Canadian AI company Cohere reported that during a security test, Alibaba’s Qwen tried to upload a file to a cloud server in Beijing, completely unprompted. The behavior was rare for Qwen, only observed once in testing, and Cohere said it could not tell whether it was “deliberate or a leftover glitch from training.” A study by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike found that when users asked DeepSeek to write code that mentions groups Beijing finds politically “sensitive,” such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, or the religious movement Falun Gong, the model became up to 50 percent more likely to write code with severe security flaws. CrowdStrike suggested that one possible cause is China’s rule that models adhere to “core socialist values.”
Despite these findings, Chinese AI is enormously popular. Last year, downloads of Chinese open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download from the Internet and run on their own hardware—surpassed those of American ones across the world. Developers have built more than 150,000 models on Alibaba’s Qwen alone. By September 2026, Chinese models handled up to 67 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a popular AI marketplace, up from around ten percent in February.
American companies have embraced them. In March, a user discovered that Cursor, a popular coding tool, had built its new model by retraining Kimi, a model from the Chinese company Moonshot AI. Airbnb, DoorDash, and the legal-services AI company Harvey use Chinese models as well. Many others likely do, too, in secret. The models are spreading even faster abroad, from Germany’s Siemens to Singapore’s national AI program to startups in Africa. The reason is simple economics: Chinese models are very cheap and very good.
Although most American AI companies do not release open-weight models, most Chinese companies do. So an American firm must pay Anthropic for each use of its unmodifiable models, but it can download Kimi for free, retrain it however it wants, and pay only for the electricity and chips to run it. Kimi also runs on a firm’s own servers, whereas Claude runs on Anthropic’s. Even if a company uses the most expensive DeepSeek model run on DeepSeek’s servers, it can produce the same amount of text as Anthropic’s top models at one-20th the cost.
In terms of capabilities, the research group Epoch AI judges Chinese models to be only about seven months behind American ones. For the price, they get the job done. And Chinese companies are now building agentic AI systems to compete with Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. In October, DeepSeek released an open-source prototype of its “Super-Agent” system.
Although AI is a new technology, Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI fit FARA’s text and history. The statute applies when a foreign principal is identified; in the case of Chinese AI models, it is the Chinese government and the CCP. The Justice Department would also have to show that the Chinese AI company acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of the principal. Chinese AI companies would qualify because they must promote CCP viewpoints and cooperate with the state’s intelligence agencies. They also receive subsidies, and party organizations are embedded in each company. This is the difference between Chinese AI and other foreign AI. For example, France’s public investment bank has a stake in the French AI company Mistral, but no French law requires Mistral to build its models to serve the French government.
Beijing will surely respond that Washington, too, has tried to control American AI companies, such as through Trump’s July 2025 executive order against “woke AI.” But that order affects only what federal agencies can procure, and a company can opt out of being a federal contractor. Meanwhile, Chinese law forces Chinese AI companies to train their models to “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.”
Every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen should carry a disclaimer.
For FARA to apply, the agent must engage in certain activities, such as attempting to influence Americans or publishing content. Chinese AI companies do both by distributing models that spread propaganda. The statute exempts purely commercial activity, but only if it is “private and nonpolitical” and does not directly promote a foreign government’s political interests. Chinese AI models engage in political speech on a government’s behalf, and the Justice Department has denied the exemption to agents of foreign governments.
After registration, the genius of the statute can kick in. Chinese AI companies must disclose extensive information to the U.S. government: their funding sources, their written contracts and oral agreements, and the influence activities they undertake. Those that fail to register or omit information face both civil and criminal penalties.
All content they disseminate must also bear a foreign-agent label: “a conspicuous statement,” in the statute’s words. The Justice Department sets the rules for what that looks like, and it has not updated them since 2003. In January 2025, the Justice Department proposed amendments to these rules to update them for the digital age. The proposed amendments would require a label on “each individual post” online, such as on social media platforms, but they do not address AI foreign agents. The final rule should require every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen to carry the disclaimer: “This was generated by an agent of the Chinese government and Chinese Communist Party.”
The standard objection is that ordinary citizens do not read disclosures. That may be true of long medical forms or Securities and Exchange Commission filings, but this label would be short. And disclosure works because experts—investors, journalists, researchers—read filings and react. When researchers and lawmakers flagged gaps in China Daily’s FARA filings, the Chinese media company disclosed that it had paid millions of dollars to The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to publish its propaganda. Payments to the Journal ended that same month. Forcing Chinese AI companies to register under FARA would also shed light on how far Chinese AI is spreading so that Americans can decide, with real data, whether they want further action, such as a ban.
American companies that use Chinese AI models can also become foreign agents if they fall under a foreign principal’s “direction or control” and engage in activities subject to FARA. This could happen in two ways: the company serves as a “CCP spokesperson,” or as a “CCP executive.”
In the first, an American company takes an unmodified Chinese AI model and lets Americans discuss political issues with it—say, via a video game character or a customer service chatbot. The model returns its usual propaganda, so the company has effectively hired a CCP spokesperson. Accordingly, it must label its outputs. Both the Justice Department and a federal court have found that rebroadcasting unmodified programming from the Russian state outlet Sputnik turns an American company into a foreign agent. Of course, American companies can avoid FARA obligations if they do not engage in any of the activities listed by the statute, such as discussing politics. A company whose public-facing Chinese AI model discusses only, say, hotel check-in times, not politics, would not be a CCP spokesperson.
In the second scenario, an American company outsources so much of its decision-making to an unmodified Chinese AI model that it has effectively hired a CCP executive. If a company hired a brilliant human strategist who always pushed Beijing’s interests, and the company followed that advice, FARA would apply. The same logic holds if an American company cedes control to the Chinese government by giving Beijing’s models high decision-making authority. Although it may sound fantastical, 64 percent of chief executives surveyed in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study say they already feel comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI input; overall, CEOs expect AI to make 48 percent of routine operational decisions autonomously by 2030. An American company that wants to avoid becoming a CCP executive must be sure not to fall under the direction or control of such models. The Justice Department should update its 2020 guidance on what constitutes “direction or control,” spelling out how much decision-making a company can outsource to AI before it has effectively hired a “CCP executive.”
The United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency.
American companies could attempt to train away the party bias in the Chinese AI models they adopt, but it is unclear whether that is even possible. Perplexity, an American AI company, trained DeepSeek to stop ignoring questions about the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and about human rights abuses in Xinjiang, but that does not fix the deeper problem of corrupt chains of thought. As these models get more capable, Chinese AI companies may also find cleverer ways to hide instructions. Or they could just stick them in the contract: some recent DeepSeek licenses prohibit modifying models to generate “inappropriate content” under Chinese law, making propaganda part of the deal. If research shows that companies can reliably remove the bias, the Justice Department and the Commerce Department should issue standards on how to train away FARA liability.
Although Pam Bondi, then the U.S. attorney general, limited criminal FARA charges in 2025 to “conduct similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors,” Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Justice Department says it is considering a new rule to “keep pace with technological change.” It should include AI foreign agents.
Of course, Washington should wield FARA’s expansive authorities with care. Frivolous prosecutions under the statute could stifle democracy. Other countries have used foreign-agent laws to shut down civil society. Since 2022, Russia has barred anyone it deems a foreign agent from holding office and organizing public events. Still, FARA is a far narrower statute, and it should stay that way. It reaches only those acting under the direction or control of a foreign principal, and it simply requires registration and labeling, leaving the speaker free to keep speaking. Chinese AI companies that are required by law to promote the CCP’s interests fit squarely within what Congress had in mind when it approved FARA in 1938.
FARA can help in the United States, but the problem is global. Chinese AI is spreading rapidly in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. That is no accident. In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping unveiled the World AI Cooperation Organization, a Shanghai-based group of 29 countries meant to make AI “beneficial, safe, and fair,” along with a development initiative to export Chinese AI worldwide. The United States and its allies cannot allow CCP executives and spokespeople to run the world’s companies and governments.
Unfortunately, the American alternatives are not particularly attractive. The most capable U.S. models are far more expensive, are largely unmodifiable, and may contain their own biases. That is why the United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency, with standards that make countries comfortable adopting allied models as their own. These should include freedom from state ideological mandates, disclosure of how the models were trained to be helpful and safe, and independent auditing.
Every member of such a compact should also adopt FARA’s wisdom by mandating labels on government-directed AI, and the United States should hold American AI companies to those transparency standards. The bloc should then release models that match China’s in price and quality (that is, around seven months behind the American frontier). Allied governments can help pay for computing power and electricity, assist in clearing regulatory hurdles, and make bulk purchase commitments to bring prices down. American companies may cut prices on their older models on their own to compete with Chinese models. If they do not, lower prices for those worse models should be the condition for the public support they receive, such as federal contracts and permission to lease federal land for data centers, just as a pharmaceutical company can charge high prices for only a set period before generic drugs arrive. The compact’s members should also use export loans and guarantees to steer developing countries toward allied AI.
By welcoming supposedly free technology from China, the United States and its allies have unwittingly invited countless foreign agents to their shores. The Foreign Agents Registration Act can strip away the disguise, and an allied AI compact can give the world a better offer.

黄仁勋事件暴露硅谷国家安全实力
中期选举的蓝色海啸刚刚登陆，特朗普政府就遭遇了另一场危机。
11月8日，黄仁勋承认（在新窗口中打开）恋情。据《纽约时报》报道，美国情报机构得出结论，他的情妇是中国国家安全部的情报人员。
此事的消息震惊了市场和监管机构。黄领导的英伟达是全球最有价值的公司，为西方与中国的技术竞争提供核心技术。他与美国政治机构关系密切，今年早些时候，他与唐纳德·特朗普总统一起乘坐空军一号对北京进行国事访问。
黄的事件显示了华盛顿与硅谷关系核心的新矛盾。私营企业高管比以往任何时候都拥有更大的权力，而旨在保护美国国家安全的机构却没有适应这种变化。
国家安全机构的设立是为了保护敏感信息。它们还保护政府决策者免受影响力的影响。针对黄的威胁集中在中国可能影响英伟达向中国出售人工智能芯片的立场，而不是控制任何特定的机密信息。
美国主要科技公司的领导人正在成为美国国家安全政策的结构性决定性人物。
世界各国政府每天都有理由将黄仁勋这样的人视为关键的地缘政治人物。
9 月，五角大楼任命 SpaceX 和特斯拉首席执行官埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 和 Anduril Industries 创始人帕尔默·拉基 (Palmer Luckey) 以及前众议院议长纽特·金里奇 (Newt Gingrich) 为 Project Meridian 的领导者。这三人将指导美国战争的未来，包括采购数千亿美元的装备。
2025 年 12 月，黄仁勋本人对 CSIS 表示，“我们国家非凡的科技产业是我们国家安全的一部分”。他的公司控制着全球 80-85% 的人工智能芯片硬件市场（在新窗口中打开），通过对基础设施的控制，将自己定位为美国实力的先锋。
硅谷高管给自己的任务是塑造美国的国家安全利益，而不是满足政府的要求，从而影响世界如何看待美国的实力。

Jensen Huang’s affair exposes Silicon Valley’s national security power
The blue tsunami of the midterms had barely landed onshore when yet another crisis hit the Trump administration.
On 8 November, Jensen Huang admitted (Opens in new window) to an affair. American intelligence agencies, according (Opens in new window) to the New York Times, have concluded that his mistress is an intelligence asset for China’s Ministry of State Security.
News of the affair shocked markets and regulators. Huang leads Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company that provides the core technology for the West’s technological competition with China. He is deeply tied with the American political apparatus, flying on Air Force One with President Donald Trump for his state visit to Beijing earlier in the year.
Huang’s affair shows a new contradiction at the heart of Washington’s relationship to Silicon Valley. Private executives have more power than ever, while the institutions designed to protect America’s national security haven’t adapted to that change.
National security apparatuses are set up to protect sensitive information. They also protect government decision-makers from influence efforts. The threat against Huang centred on the potential for China to influence Nvidia’s position on selling AI chips to China, rather than control of any particular item of classified information.
The leaders of major American technology firms are becoming structurally decisive figures in American national security policy.
Governments around the world gain reasons every day to treat people like Jensen Huang as key geopolitical figures.
In September, the Pentagon named (Opens in new window) SpaceX and Tesla chief Elon Musk and Anduril Industries founder Palmer Luckey, alongside former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, as the leaders of Project Meridian. The three will guide the future of American warfare, including acquisition of hundreds of billions of dollars of equipment.
In December 2025, Huang himself told (Opens in new window) CSIS, “our nation’s extraordinary technology industry is part of our national security”. His company, which controls 80–85% of the global market (Opens in new window) for AI chip hardware, positions itself at the vanguard of American power through its grip on the infrastructure.
Silicon Valley executives are giving themselves the job of shaping America’s national security interests rather than delivering what the government requests – in turn influencing how the world sees American power.
US President Donald Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman speak with Elon Musk, Jensen Huang and other business leaders at the US-Saudi Investment Forum, 19 November 2025, at the John F. Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts in Washington, DC (Daniel Torok/Official White House Photo)
When Musk throttled Starlink access to Ukraine’s soldiers, speculation abounded about who authorised the slowdown between Musk or Trump. The question itself proved the point, that critical decisions may be made on either side of the sector wall.
In Brazil’s presidential election, thousands of protestors gathered outside of Meta’s Sao Paolo office to decry what they saw as the company meddling in their election. In the months prior, the President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign released evidence (Opens in new window) that Meta’s platforms were promoting his opponent’s campaign and limiting Lula’s ability to reach voters. Meta accepted the result but denied any political intention behind it. The reputational damage had been done: a majority of Brazilians believe that American technology poses a risk to their national security.
A Silicon Valley executive who controls technology used by military and intelligence services may not have access to classified information, but can make consequential decisions about how the technology operates.
These companies, deeply tied to the Trump White House and at the vanguard of its definition of American power, are producing consequences that have a significance that rivals that of entire governments.
Governments around the world gain reasons every day to treat people like Jensen Huang as key geopolitical figures. This scandal shows that counterintelligence services need to account for that reality.
The FBI, the key counterintelligence service in the United States, has some efforts in place to protect private industry. They investigate attempts by foreign governments to infiltrate critical companies. Their goal is to protect classified information and hardware that could be stolen and repurposed.
As the public role that these executives play changes, so too does the problem of counterintelligence defence. A Silicon Valley executive who controls the technology used by military and intelligence services around the world may not themselves have access to classified information, but they can make consequential decisions about how the technology operates. These decisions could change what a country is capable of doing, or what technology an adversary is able to access.
Beyond the question of the appropriate counterintelligence protection for figures like Huang, there also comes the question of their political relationships.
Well before the public was made aware, Trump was informed (Opens in new window) about Huang’s relationship, including the intelligence community’s assessment that his mistress was tied to Chinese intelligence. Even after those briefings, Trump continued to speak with Huang and, once the scandal was revealed, publicly defended him.
Even once counterintelligence services adapt to the moving future, they can always be countermanded by chief executives who make political calculations about figures. Trump could have pushed Huang out, but in doing so would have alienated a key political ally, someone central to his strategic competition with China. Huang’s embrace of MAGA has also been helpful to Trump in building a political and economic support base in Silicon Valley.
The decision to do nothing with the information developed by the FBI was a political one, made because Trump saw Huang as indispensable.
This dynamic matters for every country that relies on American technology in both its civilian and public sectors. These new vulnerabilities will not stop at American borders.
The new generation of leaders taking centre stage in the United States must grapple with the seemingly insurmountable power that Silicon Valley has accumulated in the Trump era. Backlash to that very group was part of the substantial rebuke delivered by voters.
In governing, these new leaders from both parties will have to reimagine national security – including counterintelligence – to cover the public power now wielded by private actors.
Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne, where he studies the impact of AI on democracy. Previously, he served in the Biden White House for three years and as the senior adviser to Mayor Steve Benjamin.

英伟达正在调查创始人黄仁勋与一名涉嫌中国特工的关系
2026 年 11 月 11 日星期三 - 10:30 世界标准时间
该公司周日宣布，“鉴于最近有报道称创始人兼首席执行官黄仁勋已成为外国情报机构的目标”，将开始调查
英伟达董事会已对创始人兼首席执行官黄仁勋展开独立调查，原因是黄仁勋与一名华裔女商人有婚外情，美国情报部门将这名女商人与北京的间谍活动联系起来。唐纳德·特朗普总统周一表示，联邦调查局正在调查此案。没有人被指控。
该公司周日宣布，“鉴于最近有报道称创始人兼首席执行官黄仁勋已成为外国情报工作的目标”，它正在开始调查。黄承认与新加坡人工智能基础设施公司 Megaspeed 前高管 Alice Huang 的关系，尽管与她同姓，但与黄没有任何关系。据雅虎财经报道，他在给员工的备忘录中写道：“我深感抱歉。”英伟达在一份声明中表示，“没有理由相信国家安全或英伟达的机密已被泄露”。
据《纽约时报》报道，一份由国务卿马可·卢比奥监督的机密情报报告将爱丽丝·黄与中国国家安全部联系起来，并得出结论称，她寻求有关先进芯片的信息并影响其在中国的大规模分销。据美国新闻报道，她的下落不明。 NBC新闻援引消息人士的话说，司法部正在对Megaspeed进行刑事调查，该公司涉嫌向中国运送受到出口限制的Nvidia芯片；商务部已对该公司展开调查。立法者呼吁举行国会听证会。
特朗普表示，他已与黄进行过交谈，黄告诉他，他不知道该女子是间谍。 “我们会调查此事。我知道联邦调查局正在调查，我认为他会没事的，”他在白宫表示，他对这些指控感到“惊讶”。
该案影响的是人工智能行业最重要的公司。根据 Silicon Analyst 的一项研究，Nvidia 控制着 80% 到 90% 的人工智能加速器市场，并采用台湾台积电 (TSMC) 生产的加州芯片进行设计。 63岁的黄出生于台湾，在俄勒冈州长大。美国限制英伟达最先进的芯片向中国销售，黄仁勋今年游说特朗普放松这些控制；据《国家报》报道，华盛顿后来允许向中国公司出售一系列H20芯片，以换取25%的收入。
周二，美国中期选举后主要科技股大幅下跌，英伟达股价周二再次承压。

Nvidia investigates founder Jensen Huang over his relationship with an alleged Chinese agent
Wednesday, November 11th 2026 - 10:30 UTC
The company announced on Sunday that it was starting the investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”
Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into founder and chief executive Jensen Huang after it emerged that he had an extramarital relationship with a businesswoman of Chinese origin whom US intelligence services link to Beijing’s espionage. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is investigating the case. No one has been charged.
The company announced on Sunday that it was starting the investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Huang acknowledged the relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed, to whom he is not related despite sharing a surname. “I am deeply sorry,” he wrote in a memo to employees, according to Yahoo Finance. Nvidia said in a statement that it has no “reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia’s secrets have been compromised”.
According to The New York Times, a classified intelligence report, overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, linked Alice Huang to China’s Ministry of State Security and concluded that she sought information on advanced chips and to influence their large-scale distribution in China. Her whereabouts are unknown, according to U.S. News. A source cited by NBC News also said the Justice Department is conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, which is suspected of shipping export-restricted Nvidia chips to China; the Commerce Department already had an inquiry open into the company. Lawmakers have called for a congressional hearing.
Trump, who said he had spoken with Huang, said Huang told him he did not know the woman was a spy. “We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is investigating, and I think he’ll come out fine,” he said at the White House, where he said he was “amazed” by the allegations.
The case affects the most important company in the artificial intelligence industry. Nvidia controls between 80% and 90% of the AI accelerator market, according to a Silicon Analyst study, and designs in California chips that Taiwan’s TSMC manufactures. Huang, 63, was born in Taiwan and raised in Oregon. The United States restricts sales of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China, and Huang lobbied Trump this year to ease those controls; according to El País, Washington later allowed a series of H20 chips to be sold to Chinese companies in exchange for 25% of the revenue.
Nvidia shares came under renewed pressure on Tuesday, in a week when major tech stocks fell sharply after the US midterm elections.

在反情报简报会上，政府工作人员、军官和情报人员都被灌输了这样一句话：“如果她是 10 分，而你是 5 分，那么她就是间谍！”或者，正如美国陆军反情报司令部在情人节发布的那样：“不需要数学家就能算出‘10 + 5 = 美人计’。”这个非常漂亮的女人突然对你平凡的存在感兴趣，可能别有用心，这就是信息。
黄仁勋的生活肯定不是典型的——他是一位亿万富翁，是 Nvidia 虚张声势的首席执行官，Nvidia 是 21 世纪最热门、最具地缘政治影响力的公司之一。他当然意识到自己有可能与情报人员发生冲突。事实上，很难想象世界上有多少公司会成为外国情报机构更优先的目标。
所有这些都使得本周震动股市的消息更加令人惊讶。黄是如何卷入一场将不忠、国际间谍活动、特朗普政府和价值数万亿美元的人工智能行业的经济庞然大物混合在一起的间谍丑闻的？

正如人们所预料的那样，中国否认有任何以黄仁勋为中心的邪恶阴谋。中国外交部发言人周一表示，“所谓中国间谍的说法完全是无端猜测，纯属污蔑抹黑”。
但据《纽约时报》和《金融时报》报道，美国情报官员还声称，黄乐（又名黄乐）正在向中国国家安全部情报机构汇报工作。周一，Megaspeed 在 LinkedIn 上表示，美国当局“没有发现任何涉及非法转让芯片或任何非法活动的证据”。 （到目前为止，没有任何迹象表明曾任中国国家记者的黄爱丽是中国情报部门的雇员或“官员”；她被认为是一个“资产”，一个为情报机构提供帮助的局外人，有时是为了报酬，有时不是。）

【原文 English Original】
China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway | WIRED
There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives, is the message.
Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies.
All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry?
The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern.
As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said, “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.”
But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times, US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.)
China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes. “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation.
Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians, including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “LinkedIn espionage”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives.
Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business. The Biden administration had sharply limited the export of cutting-edge chips globally to slow China’s development of AI, but Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen those restrictions.
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Donald Trump denied having prior knowledge of Alice Huang’s potential espionage. “I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that,” Trump said. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” On Tuesday, the Times reported that Marco Rubio had briefed Trump in May, right before Jensen Huang joined the President on Air Force One for a trip to China.
The veracity of Trump's claims will surely be investigated, especially in the context of the famous Watergate maxim: “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Nvidia’s CEO has been publicly linked to the Megaspeed executive since at least 2024 and Alice’s husband, Kang Weigh, has reportedly known Jensen since the 2010s. WIRED’s Lauren Goode reported on Monday that Jensen Huang, starting in 2025, hired Risa Heller’s crisis communications firm, which is well-versed in handling public sex scandals. This spring, secretary of state Marco Rubio evidently helped craft a classified memo inside the administration warning officials about Jensen Huang’s potentially compromising relationship.
Jensen Huang—who has developed an important reputation as AI’s #1 cheerleader at the frontier of AI labs—is now stuck in an awkward situation. Is he an idiot, unaware that his paramour might have been a foreign intelligence asset? Merely reckless with his own reputation, fiduciary responsibility to Nvidia, and the technological security of the United States? Or a witting accomplice to undermining US national security?
Regardless of the truth, Nvidia loses. Shareholders have ridden a roller-coaster that has seen Nvidia’s stock rise by about 600 percent over the past five years, becoming the world’s second-most valuable company. In the past month, the stock has plummeted by a quarter. The disaster for Nvidia is just beginning, it seems, as lawsuits loom, including by its own shareholders.
Similarly, the Trump administration is likely to face real questions from the newly Democratic congress: When were the president and other top officials briefed about this intelligence threat? What communication, if any, did they make to Nvidia and to whom? Should more have been done by US intelligence to block Alice Huang from having access to Nvidia and its CEO?
The fact that Megaspeed is a major customer of Nvidia makes everything more complicated. Indeed, reports have circulated for at least a year that the US was concerned that Megaspeed was diverting chips to Chinese intelligence agencies, an allegation that could have massive consequences for the global AI race. Bloomberg this week reported that Megaspeed's subsidiaries have purchased billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and that an audit requested by the US government last year found that Megaspeed couldn’t initially account for some 50,000 chips it had purchased.
Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Huang and President Trump developed a uniquely close professional relationship. They’ve met multiple times as Huang has pushed to loosen Biden-era export controls, which Trump has repeatedly relaxed; Huang has donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project; while en route to Beijing earlier this year with a delegation of tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Tim Cook, Trump’s Air Force One actually made a special stop in Alaska to pick up Huang; Huang also attended a White House state dinner for Chinese president Xi Jinping and Trump, who in turn, awarded him a National Medal of Science earlier this fall.
The implication that Trump knew and did nothing for a year would make this one of the greatest counterintelligence failures of the past decade. There will be consequences: Across history, many have gone to prison for honeypot scandals; a former adviser was arrested just last year in a similar plot; though he was acquitted of committing economic espionage, he was convicted for making false statements to investigators.
Even in normal circumstances, corporate America’s tolerance of CEO misbehavior has shrunken dramatically. In recent years, CEOs at companies as varied as Nestlé, Kohl’s, BP, NBCUniversal, and the railroad Norfolk Southern have all resigned or been forced out after inappropriate relationships that violated company standards.
If Nvidia were any other company and Jensen Huang any other CEO, the facts of the scandal currently known would be enough to topple some heads. But Trump is still president, and November is only a third over. It’s not even clear that this will rank as the biggest scandal of the month—but it should.

印度9月石油进口量创历史新高，其中三分之一以上由俄罗斯供应
进口量较 8 月平均增长 20%，达到 540 万桶/日
莫斯科，11 月 11 日。/塔斯社/。 2026 年 9 月，俄罗斯仍然是中国和印度最大的石油供应国，但由于两国石油进口增加，其份额略有下降。与此同时，欧佩克报告称，印度的石油进口总量达到了创纪录的水平。
报告称，具体而言，9月份俄罗斯占印度石油进口量的35%，低于8月份的45%，而伊拉克和沙特阿拉伯各占10%。
在炼油厂吞吐量强劲的推动下，印度 9 月份原油进口总量创下历史新高：进口量较 8 月份平均增长 20%，达到 540 万桶/日。这比 2025 年 9 月的进口量增加了 13%。
此外，9月份中国石油进口继续增长，增幅超过1.5%，达到904万桶/日。俄罗斯仍然是中国最大的石油供应国，占报告期内进口总量的28%，低于上月的30%，而巴西和伊拉克的供应量分别为14%和13%。
9月份中国石油产品出口量环比增长17%，同比增长36%至180万桶/日。欧佩克表示，柴油和燃料油的出货量增长尤其急剧。

India's oil imports up to record level in September with over third supplied by Russia
Imports rose by 20% on average compared to August to 5.4 mln barrels per day
MOSCOW, November 11. /TASS/. Russia remained the largest oil supplier to China and India in September 2026, though its share declined slightly amid rising oil imports by both countries. Meanwhile, India’s total oil imports reached a record volume, OPEC reported.
Specifically, Russia accounted for 35% of India’s oil imports in September, down from 45% in August, while Iraq and Saudi Arabia each supplied 10%, the report said.
India’s total crude oil imports reached a record high in September driven by strong refinery throughput: imports rose by 20% on average compared to August to 5.4 mln barrels per day. This represents a 13% increase over the volume imported in September 2025.
Moreover, China’s oil imports continued to rise in September, increasing by over 1.5% to 9.04 mln barrels per day. Russia remained the largest oil supplier to China, accounting for 28% of total imports in the reporting period, down from 30% in the previous month, while Brazil and Iraq supplied 14% and 13%, respectively.
China also increased its exports of petroleum products by 17% in September month-on-month, and by 36% year-on-year to 1.8 mln barrels per day. Shipments of diesel fuel and fuel oil saw a particularly sharp increase, OPEC said.

德黑兰感谢俄罗斯和中国在联合国安理会采取的历史性立场
伊朗驻俄罗斯大使馆公使衔参赞阿夫辛·帕奇扎德表示，“即使是欧洲国家也不支持对伊朗进行军事侵略”
莫斯科，11 月 11 日。/塔斯社/。伊朗驻俄罗斯大使馆公使衔参赞阿夫辛·帕奇扎德表示，莫斯科和北京在联合国安理会上采取的共同和统一立场，特别是在伊朗问题上，确实具有历史意义。他补充说，伊朗伊斯兰共和国赞赏这种做法，并为此向俄罗斯表示感谢。
他在国际集体安全论坛上表示：“俄罗斯和中国近几个月在联合国安理会采取的立场，就国际法范围内针对美国单方面行动采取的步骤而言，具有历史意义。我们感谢俄罗斯支持伊朗的立场，这反映了两国之间稳定和根深蒂固的关系。”
帕奇扎德指出：“在最近的战争和与之相关的事件中，一直持续到今天，外交舞台上也得到了亚洲伊斯兰共和国的支持。世界上许多国家，例如俄罗斯和欧亚国家，在第一天就谴责了对伊朗的袭击，并将其描述为非法的。”
他强调，尽管如此，“即使是欧洲国家也不支持对伊朗进行军事侵略”，而美国则试图通过向联合国安理会提交旨在延长武器供应禁运的美以决议草案为其非法行为奠定法律基础。这位外交官补充说，是俄罗斯和中国行使否决权阻止了该草案。

俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司11月第五次更新对中国的每日天然气供应量记录
莫斯科，11 月 11 日。/塔斯社/。俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司宣布，今年11月第五次更新了每日向中国供应管道天然气的记录。
声明称：“自11月初以来，俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司第五次刷新了通过西伯利亚力量管道向中国供应天然气的历史最高水平。新纪录是在11月10日创下的。”
俄罗斯天然气供应是根据俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司与中国石油天然气集团公司之间的长期购销协议交付的。俄罗斯副总理诺瓦克此前表示，今年俄罗斯将通过“西伯利亚力量”管道向中国供应390亿立方米天然气。
2025年，俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司成为中国最大的天然气出口商。通过西伯利亚力量管道的供应量达到388亿立方米，比最初的合同义务多了8亿立方米。
西伯利亚力量是俄罗斯东部最大的天然气输送系统，每年天然气出口能力为380亿立方米。根据俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司与中国石油天然气集团公司于2014年签署的为期30年的合同，俄罗斯第一条通过东线管道向中国供应天然气的工程于2019年12月开始。合同期内天然气供应总量将超过1万亿立方米，合同价值达4000亿美元。

Gazprom updates record daily gas supplies to China for fifth time in November
MOSCOW, November 11. /TASS/. Gazprom has updated its record for daily pipeline gas supplies to China for the fifth time this November, the company announced.
"For the fifth time since the beginning of November, Gazprom has updated its all-time high for daily gas supplies to China via the Power of Siberia pipeline. The new record was set on November 10," the statement said.
Russian gas supplies are delivered under a long-term purchase and sale agreement between Gazprom and CNPC. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak previously stated that Russia would supply 39 billion cubic meters of gas to China via the Power of Siberia pipeline this year.
In 2025, Gazprom became the largest gas exporter to China. Supplies via the Power of Siberia pipeline reached 38.8 billion cubic meters, exceeding initial contractual obligations by 800 million cubic meters.
Power of Siberia is the largest gas transmission system in eastern Russia, with an export capacity of 38 billion cubic meters of gas per year. The first pipeline supplies of Russian gas to China via the eastern route began in December 2019 under a 30-year contract signed between Gazprom and China’s CNPC in 2014. Total supplies over the contract's duration will exceed 1 trillion cubic meters of gas, with the contract valued at $400 billion.

MOSCOW (Sputnik) - The scandal around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman whom US intelligence suspects of working for China underscores the need to stay diligent, but will not undermine US contacts with China, US Ambassador to China David Perdue said.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Monday that claims of Chinese spying on Nvidia were purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.
"The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent... What we're doing with China is bumpy right now. We have some areas of disagreement, but we have engagement… We could potentially have five top-to-top engagements within fifteen months. I can't find time in history where we had two presidents of two great countries get together that frequently," Perdue told Bloomberg,
He was asked whether the suspected espionage case could harm bilateral relations amid preparations for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, scheduled for November 18-19.
The New York Times reported on November 6 that Chinese business executive Alice Huang had a close relationship with Jensen Huang and was an "asset" of China's Ministry of State Security. Jensen Huang confessed to having an extramarital affair. Nvidia announced the start of an independent probe. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said that Huang intended to continue in his position.

United States Section, International Boundary and Water Commission, United States and Mexico (USIBWC).ACTION: Notice of availability.
The USIBWC hereby gives notice that the Draft Environmental Assessment (EA) and Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) for the Reconstruction of the Fort Hancock-El Porvenir International Bridge, Rio Grande Rectification Project, Hudspeth County, Texas is available.
Elizabeth Verdecchia, Natural Resources Specialist, Telephone: (915) 832-4701, email: elizabeth.verdecchia@ibwc.gov.
The electronic version of the Draft EA and FONSI is available at the USIBWC web page: https://www.ibwc.gov/​reports-studies/​eis-ea-public-comment/​. Public comments may be submitted to Elizabeth Verdecchia, Natural Resources Specialist, USIBWC, 4191 N Mesa, El Paso, Texas 79902; email: elizabeth.verdecchia@ibwc.gov.
The USIBWC is proposing to construct a new bridge section on the U.S. side of the Fort Hancock—El Porvenir International Bridge that would tie-in to the Mexican section of the bridge, in order to address structural and safety issues with the bridge. Pursuant to Section 102(2)(c) of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) of 1969, as amended, and the USIBWC Operational Procedures for Implementing Section 102 of NEPA, published in the Federal Register September 2, 1981, USIBWC developed a Draft EA that analyzed the Action Alternative (Preferred Alternative) and the No Action Alternative. The Action Alternative—U.S. Side Rebuild to Same Profile would construct a new bridge section on the U.S. side to address with the structural integrity of the substructure and bridge deck. The new bridge section on the U.S. side would tie-in to the Mexican section of the bridge, which is in good condition. The new bridge section would generally match the existing bridge with regard to having the same height and width, similar roadway and sidewalk, but with an improved floodgate. Under the No Action Alternative, USIBWC would not construct a new bridge section, and the safety issues would not be addressed.
Potential impacts on natural, cultural, and other resources were evaluated. A Finding of No Significant Impact for the Proposed Action, based on a review of the facts and analyses contained in the EA. An environmental impact statement will not be prepared.
USIBWC Deputy Chief Counsel, International Boundary and Water Commission, United States Section.

日本家具巨头 Nitori 称黑客窃取了 3760 万条客户记录
日本家具巨头 Nitori 称黑客窃取了 3760 万条客户记录
日本家具巨头 Nitori 称黑客窃取了 3760 万条客户记录
日本主要家具和家居饰品零售商 Nitori 发现攻击者访问了其网络上的系统，可能窃取了 3762 万条客户记录。
11 月 6 日检测到入侵，该公司阻止了未经授权的访问。然而，对该事件的调查显示，攻击者很可能自 10 月中旬以来就已经访问过该系统。
Nitori 通常被称为“日本的宜家”，是一家大型家具和家居用品零售商，在日本经营 879 家商店，并在中国、韩国、台湾、泰国、新加坡和香港经营另外 219 家商店。该公司年收入为 58 亿美元。
根据该公司的通知，该事件影响到通过 Nitori 官方商店和网上商店下订单的个人客户、企业会员和非会员。
该公司在通知中表示：“2026 年 11 月 6 日，我们确认第三方未经授权访问了我们公司管理的系统。”
“我们迄今为止的调查显示，我们服务器上保存的多达 3762 万条个人信息记录可能已被外部泄露。”
潜在暴露的信息可能包括以下数据类型：
个人会员和购买者：会员号码、姓名、电子邮件地址、邮寄地址、电话号码、出生日期和性别。
企业会员：会员编号、公司名称、部门名称、代表姓名、公司地址和电话号码，以及联系人姓名、电子邮件地址和电话号码。
在线订单：通过 Nitori Net 和电子商务市场上的 Nitori 官方商店购买的订单信息。
该公司表示，此次事件中注册会员的账户密码和信用卡信息并未被泄露。
Nitori 表示，它立即阻止了攻击者的访问，解决了系统中的漏洞，并加强了威胁监控，以防止未来发生类似事件。
该公司警告可能受影响的客户，泄露的信息可能会被用于网络钓鱼攻击和诈骗，并敦促他们谨慎行事。
该公告强调，Nitori 绝不会通过电子邮件或电话交谈询问客户的密码、信用卡号或 PIN 码。
Nitori 已通知日本个人信息保护委员会、警方和其他相关部门，并承诺通过电子邮件或邮寄方式直接通知受影响的客户。
BleepingComputer 已联系 Nitori 询问有关该事件的问题，我们将在收到回复后更新这篇文章。
11/11 更新 - Nitori 发言人告诉 BleepingComputer，他们目前正在调查原因，包括是否涉及勒索软件，并与外部网络安全专家合作。该公司尚未确定受影响的客户数量。

Japanese furniture giant Nitori says hackers stole 37.6M customer records
Japanese furniture giant Nitori says hackers stole 37.6M customer records
Japanese furniture giant Nitori says hackers stole 37.6M customer records
Nitori, a major Japanese furniture and home accessories retailer, discovered that an attacker accessed a system on its network and may have stolen 37.62 million customer records.
The intrusion was detected on November 6, and the company blocked the unauthorized access. However, an investigation into the incident revealed that the attacker likely had access to the system since mid-October.
Nitori, often called the “IKEA of Japan,” is a major furniture and home furnishings retailer that operates 879 stores in Japan and another 219 stores across China, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore, and Hong Kong. The firm has an annual revenue of $5.8 billion.
According to the company's notification, the incident impacts individual customers, corporate members, and non-members who placed orders through official Nitori stores and online shops.
“On November 6, 2026, we confirmed unauthorized access by a third party to a system managed by our company,” [machine translated] the company says in the notification
“Our investigation to date has revealed that up to 37.62 million records of personal information held on our servers may have been leaked externally.”
The potentially exposed information may include the following data types:
Individual members and purchasers: Membership numbers, names, email addresses, postal addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, and gender.
Corporate members: Membership numbers, company names, department names, representatives’ names, company addresses and telephone numbers, and contact persons’ names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.
Online orders: Order information for purchases through Nitori Net and official Nitori shops on e-commerce marketplaces.
The company specified that account passwords of registered members and credit card information were not exposed in this incident.
Nitori says it promptly blocked the attacker’s access, addressed vulnerabilities in its systems, and strengthened threat monitoring to prevent similar incidents in the future.
The company warned potentially impacted customers that the compromised information could be leveraged in phishing attacks and scamming attempts against, and urged them to exercise caution.
The announcement emphasizes that Nitori will never ask customers for their password, credit card number, or PIN by email or in phone conversations.
Nitori has informed Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission, the police, and other relevant authorities, and has promised to notify affected customers directly by email or post.
BleepingComputer has contacted Nitori with questions about the incident, and we will update this post when we get a reply.
Update 11/11 - A Nitori spokesperson told BleepingComputer that they are currently investigating the cause, including whether ransomware was involved, and cooperate with external cybersecurity experts. The company has not yet determined the number of customers impacted.

Qubole 是一个企业云数据处理和分析平台，可帮助公司管理大型数据集并运行机器学习工作负载。它还提供 AWS 集成以允许计算资源管理。
公司可以通过创建跨账户 IAM 角色来授予 Qubole 等第三方提供商对其 AWS 资源的访问权限。信任策略确定哪些外部 AWS 账户可以担任这些角色，并设置权限来定义允许的资源和操作。
云安全公司 Wiz 的研究人员解释说，外部提供商使用 AWS 的 STS AssumeRole API 来获取用于访问客户在云中的资源的临时凭证。
在数据安全和治理公司 Sentra 分享了在其一些客户环境中观察到的可疑活动的信息后，Wiz 开始调查此次攻击。调查还包括网络安全公司 Mandiant。
研究人员发现，攻击者入侵了两名 Qubole IAM 用户，并在多个客户的 AWS 账户中承担了原本未使用的角色，这些账户之前已配置为信任 Qubole 的账户，从而授予他们在角色权限范围内的访问权限。
Wiz 表示，攻击者随后调查了云资源，从 AWS Secrets Manager 和 SSM Parameter Store 检索机密，并读取 Lambda 环境变量。
然后，他们使用 TruffleHog 工具来验证发现的 AWS 密钥、Microsoft Entra ID 客户端密钥和 Okta 客户端凭证。
一旦获得更深入的访问权限，他们就会从 AWS 环境中所有可访问的 S3 存储桶中下载数据，采用机会主义方法，而不是仔细针对特定数据。
“该顺序在各个环境中都是一致的：假设一个角色，调用 ListBuckets 查看该角色可以到达的内容，调用 ListObjects 和 HeadObject 枚举和检查内容，然后调用 GetObject 下载它们，”Wiz 解释道。
该报告没有具体说明用于破坏 Qubole 账户的确切方法或下游受害者的数量。然而，Sentra 证实，仅一名客户就有数十名受害者和数百万个文件被盗。
Sentra 表示，攻击者行动迅速，在 7 分钟内收集了 100 个密码和密钥。
BleepingComputer 找不到 Qubole 关于此事件的公告。我们已向该公司发送电子邮件以获取有关此次攻击的更多信息，并等待他们的回复。
建议潜在受影响的管理员从 10 月 1 日起检查 CloudTrail 是否存在来自 Qubole 的 AWS 账户的可疑访问，调查后续的机密和 S3 访问，轮换暴露的凭证，并撤销活动角色会话。
还建议删除未使用的集成并限制剩余角色的权限、可信身份和允许的源网络。

【原文 English Original】
Hackers exploit trusted AWS access to breach multiple cloud environments
Hackers exploit trusted AWS access to breach multiple cloud environments
Hackers exploit trusted AWS access to breach multiple cloud environments
A threat actor used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials for a Qubole big data platform's AWS account to access and exfiltrate data from multiple customers' AWS environments.
The campaign ran between October 14 and 26, and affected tens of companies whose AWS environments had IAM roles configured to trust an AWS account associated with Qubole.
Qubole is an enterprise cloud data processing and analytics platform that helps companies manage large datasets and run machine learning workloads. It also offers AWS integration to allow computing resource management.
Companies can grant third-party providers such as Qubole access to their AWS resources by creating cross-account IAM roles. Trust policies determine which external AWS accounts can take these roles, and permissions are set to define the resources and actions allowed.
Researchers at cloud security company Wiz explain that external providers use AWS’s STS AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for accessing customers' resources in the cloud.
Wiz started to investigate the attack after data security and governance company Sentra shared information about suspicious activity observed in some of its customers' environments. The investigation also included cybersecurity company Mandiant.
The researchers found that the attacker had compromised two Qubole IAM users and assumed otherwise unused roles in multiple customers’ AWS accounts that had previously been configured to trust Qubole’s account, granting them access within the role’s permissions.
Wiz says the attacker then surveyed cloud resources, retrieved secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store, and read Lambda environment variables.
They then used the TruffleHog tool to validate discovered AWS keys, Microsoft Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.
Once they gained deeper access, they downloaded data from all accessible S3 buckets in the AWS environment, following an opportunistic approach rather than carefully targeting specific data.
“The sequence was consistent across environments: assume a role, call ListBuckets to see what the role could reach, call ListObjects and HeadObject to enumerate and inspect the contents, then call GetObject to download them,” Wiz explains.
The report does not specify the exact method used to compromise the Qubole accounts or the number of downstream victims. However, Sentra confirmed dozens of victims and millions of files stolen from one customer alone.
Sentra says the attacker moved quickly and collected secrets at a rate of 100 passwords and keys in seven minutes.
BleepingComputer could not find a public announcement from Qubole about this incident. We have emailed the firm for more information about the attack and await their response.
Potentially impacted administrators are advised to review CloudTrail from October 1 onward for suspicious access from Qubole’s AWS account, investigate subsequent secret and S3 access, rotate exposed credentials, and revoke active role sessions.
It is also recommended to remove unused integrations and restrict remaining roles’ permissions, trusted identities, and permitted source networks.
Update 11/11 - An AWS spokesperson sent BleepingComputer the below comment:
"AWS services were not compromised by this issue and operated as designed. The activity describes how threat actors used credentials associated with a third-party provider to access some AWS customers' accounts by assuming IAM roles those customers had configured to trust that provider. As always, we recommend all customers follow security, identity, and compliance best practices, including regularly reviewing cross-account IAM roles, removing access for integrations no longer in use, granting least-privilege permissions, and adding conditions such as source IP restrictions to role trust policies. AWS customers who suspect or become aware of unauthorized activity in their accounts should follow guidance for remediating potentially compromised credentials or contact AWS Support with any questions or concerns about the security of their account." — AWS spokesperson

黑客在 AWS 凭证盗窃攻击中使用 AntiFox AI 代理
黑客在 AWS 凭证盗窃攻击中使用 AntiFox AI 代理
黑客在 AWS 凭证盗窃攻击中使用 AntiFox AI 代理
攻击者正在使用阿里云托管开源代理渗透测试平台 AntiFox 的自我管理实例，以针对 Web 服务和 AWS 环境。
托管 AntiFox 的基础设施被用于各种恶意活动，包括漏洞利用、Webshel​​l 部署、凭证验证、配置发现和 AWS 秘密收集。
AntiFox 最初是作为 ARTEX 0.1.1 的一个分支创建的，具有中文界面，允许用户部署人工智能代理并自动执行常见的渗透测试任务，例如映射暴露的服务和探测目标端点的漏洞。
Arctic Wolf 的安全研究人员观察到，阿里云上托管的与 AntiFox 相关的恶意基础设施使用有效的 AWS 身份（包括 IAM 用户，在某些情况下还假设了 EC2 角色）向 Amazon Web Services API 发出经过身份验证的请求。
Arctic Wolf 表示：“在最近观察到的几起入侵事件中，托管 AntiFox 接口的阿里云系统与针对面向互联网的 Web 服务和相关 AWS 环境的已确认的恶意行为有关。”
报告中强调的一个案例涉及在暴露于互联网的 IIS 服务器上部署 ASPX Webshel​​l、执行操作系统命令、访问应用程序设置和数据库连接字符串以及将配置和日志文件复制到可通过 Web 访问的目录。
攻击者还使用有效的 IAM 凭证和 EC2 角色来探测 Amazon Web Services (AWS) 端点。研究人员指出，在一次入侵中，他们循环使用了多个身份，并在大约 30 分钟内发出了数百个 API 请求。
尽管大多数尝试都被阻止，但攻击者在某些情况下成功并获得了生产秘密。
在另一起事件中，攻击者使用有效的 AWS 身份读取、复制和删除 S3 对象。
Arctic Wolf 的报告包括针对防御者的狩猎指南和建议，其中包括将 IIS Webshel​​l 活动与异常的 AWS 访问相关联，以及在拒绝爆发时审查成功的 API 调用。
研究人员还建议撤销受影响的 AWS 会话和密钥，并轮换通过应用程序文件公开的凭证。
AntiFox 的调查结果是在最近涉及 ARTEX AI 的攻击之后发布的，ARTEX AI 是中国开发的另一个代理渗透测试框架，在用于攻击韩国银行后，该框架已被封闭。
CrowdStrike 还将 ARTEX 与一项网络间谍活动联系起来，在该活动中，中国黑客组织 Vapor Panda 针对 14 个国家的 200 多个组织进行了攻击。
目前，AntiFox 仍可在 GitHub 上使用，并已更新至 2.0 版本，改进了该工具记录和报告结果的方式。
其发布者禁止在现实世界的渗透测试或安全练习中使用该工具来攻击实时系统，或者用于破坏性或非法活动，但他们没有描述任何强制执行这些限制的技术控制措施。

【原文 English Original】
Hackers use AntiFox AI agents in AWS credential-theft attacks
Hackers use AntiFox AI agents in AWS credential-theft attacks
Hackers use AntiFox AI agents in AWS credential-theft attacks
Attackers are using Alibaba Cloud to host self-managed instances of AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration testing platform, to target web services and AWS environments.
The infrastructure hosting AntiFox was used for various malicious activities, including vulnerability exploitation, webshell deployment, credential validation, configuration discovery, and AWS secret harvesting.
Initially created as a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, AntiFox has a Chinese-language interface and lets users deploy AI agents and automate common penetration-testing tasks, such as mapping exposed services and probing target endpoints for vulnerabilities.
Security researchers at Arctic Wolf observed malicious AntiFox-linked infrastructure hosted on Alibaba Cloud using valid AWS identities, including IAM users and, in some cases, assumed EC2 roles, to make authenticated requests to Amazon Web Services APIs.
“In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments,” Arctic Wolf says.
One case highlighted in the report involved deploying an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed IIS server, executing OS commands, accessing application settings and database connection strings, and copying configuration and log files to a web-accessible directory.
The attacker also used valid IAM credentials and EC2 roles to probe Amazon Web Services (AWS) endpoints. In one intrusion, they cycled through multiple identities and made hundreds of API requests in about 30 minutes, the researchers note.
Although most of these attempts were blocked, the attacker was successful in some cases and obtained production secrets.
In a separate incident, the attackers used a valid AWS identity to read, copy, and delete S3 objects.
Arctic Wolf's report includes hunting guidance and recommendations for defenders that include correlating IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access and reviewing successful API calls within bursts of denials.
The researchers also recommend revoking affected AWS sessions and keys and rotating credentials exposed through application files.
The AntiFox findings follow recent attacks involving ARTEX AI, another agentic penetration-testing framework developed in China that went closed-source after it was used in attacks on South Korean banks.
CrowdStrike also linked ARTEX to a cyberespionage campaign in which the Chinese hacking group Vapor Panda targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries.
For now, AntiFox remains available on GitHub, where it has been updated to version 2.0, which improves how the tool documents and reports findings.
Its publishers prohibit using the tool against live systems, in real-world penetration tests or security exercises, or for destructive or illegal activity, but they do not describe any technical controls that enforce those restrictions.

title: CISA flags Cisco BroadWorks flaw as actively exploited in attacks
zh_title: CISA 将 Cisco BroadWorks 缺陷标记为在攻击中被积极利用
summary: CISA 将思科 BroadWorks 缺陷标记为在攻击中被积极利用 CISA 将思科 BroadWorks 缺陷标记为在攻击中被积极利用 CISA 将思科 BroadWorks 缺陷标记为在攻击中被积极利用 美国网络安全和基础设施安全局 (CISA) 周二警告称，黑客现在正在利用思科 BroadWorks 的高严重性漏洞进行攻击。 Cisco BroadWorks 是一个云统一通信 (UC) 软件平台和底层引擎，允许电信运营商和托管服务提供商 (MSP) 提供品牌云 PBX、语音和协作服务
content:
CISA 将 Cisco BroadWorks 缺陷标记为在攻击中被积极利用
CISA 将 Cisco BroadWorks 缺陷标记为在攻击中被积极利用
CISA 将 Cisco BroadWorks 缺陷标记为在攻击中被积极利用
美国网络安全和基础设施安全局 (CISA) 周二警告称，黑客目前正在利用思科 BroadWorks 的一个高严重性漏洞进行攻击。
Cisco BroadWorks 是一个云统一通信 (UC) 软件平台和底层引擎，允许电信运营商和托管服务提供商 (MSP) 向企业客户提供品牌云 PBX、语音和协作服务。
该安全漏洞被追踪为 CVE-2026-20320，源于开放客户端接口 (OCI) XML 解析器中对 XML 外部实体 (XXE) 引用漏洞的不当限制，该漏洞可能允许未经身份验证的远程攻击者通过发送恶意制作的 XML 消息从易受攻击的系统中读取敏感配置信息。
“此漏洞的存在是因为默认情况下允许外部实体解析，导致 XML 条目解析不正确。攻击者可以通过向开放客户端接口 - 配置 (OCI-P) 服务发送精心设计的 XML 消息来利用此漏洞，”思科在 8 月份修补该漏洞时解释道。
CISA 于周二将 CVE-2026-20320 标记为被积极利用的漏洞，并将其添加到其已知被利用的漏洞 (KEV) 目录中，并命令联邦民事行政部门 (FCEB) 机构根据《约束性操作指令》(BOD) 26-04 的规定，在 11 月 24 日之前的两周内确保其系统的安全。
尽管 BOD 26-04 仅针对联邦机构，但 CISA 敦促所有安全团队（包括私营部门的安全团队）优先考虑针对此漏洞的补丁，以保护其网络免受持续攻击。
它警告说：“这些类型的漏洞是恶意网络行为者的常见攻击媒介，并对联邦企业构成重大风险。” “虽然 BOD 26-04 仅适用于 FCEB 机构，但 CISA 鼓励所有组织采用基于风险的漏洞管理并优先修复 KEV 目录漏洞。”
虽然 CISA 没有透露攻击者在野外利用 CVE-2026-20320 的更多细节，但威胁情报公司 Malbear Labs 周末表示，一名中文威胁参与者在越狱的 DeepSeek Flash 人工智能模型的帮助下利用了该漏洞，对一家欧洲电信提供商和 13 个使用其数据中心和云基础设施的组织进行了攻击。
此次攻击主要针对电信提供商的 BroadWorks XSP（扩展服务平台），Malbear Labs 发现 BroadWorks 配置服务器（存储所有用户的订户配置）也通过未经身份验证的目录列表暴露。
Malbear Labs 表示：“该代理利用了 CVE-2026-20320，这是 BroadWorks OCI XML 解析器中未经身份验证的 XXE。对端口 2208 的精心设计的 OCI 请求会导致 XML 解析器从服务器文件系统读取任意文件，并且不需要事先进行身份验证。”
“代理从 XSP 主机恢复了系统身份私钥、三个 SSL 凭证集和三个已确认证书匹配的附加私钥。BroadWorks 平台使用系统身份密钥在其自己的组件之间进行身份验证；拥有它可以在组件间通信中模拟 XSP。”

【原文 English Original】
CISA flags Cisco BroadWorks flaw as actively exploited in attacks
CISA flags Cisco BroadWorks flaw as actively exploited in attacks
CISA flags Cisco BroadWorks flaw as actively exploited in attacks
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned on Tuesday that hackers are now exploiting a high-severity Cisco BroadWorks vulnerability in attacks.
Cisco BroadWorks is a cloud unified communications (UC) software platform and the underlying engine allowing telecom carriers and managed service providers (MSPs) to provide branded cloud PBX, voice, and collaboration services to business customers.
Tracked as CVE-2026-20320, the security flaw stems from an improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) reference weakness in the Open Client Interface (OCI) XML Parser that can allow unauthenticated, remote attackers to read sensitive configuration information from vulnerable systems by sending maliciously crafted XML messages.
"This vulnerability exists because XML entries are improperly parsed due to external entity resolution being allowed by default. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted XML message to the Open Client Interface - Provisioning (OCI-P) service," Cisco explained when it patched the bug in August.
CISA flagged CVE-2026-20320 as actively exploited and added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Tuesday, ordering Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to secure their systems within two weeks, by November 24, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.
Although BOD 26-04 targets only federal agencies, CISA urged all security teams, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patches for this vulnerability to defend their networks against ongoing attacks.
"These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," it warned. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities."
While CISA didn't share more details on attackers exploiting CVE-2026-20320 in the wild, threat intelligence firm Malbear Labs said over the weekend that a Chinese-speaking threat actor has exploited the flaw with the help of a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash artificial intelligence model in attacks targeting a European telecommunications provider and thirteen organizations that used its data centers and cloud infrastructure.
The attack focused on the telecom provider's BroadWorks XSP (eXtended Services Platform), and Malbear Labs found that the BroadWorks Provisioning Server (which stores subscriber configuration for all users) was also exposed via an unauthenticated directory listing.
"The agent exploited CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in the BroadWorks OCI XML parser. A crafted OCI request to port 2208 causes the XML parser to read arbitrary files from the server filesystem and no prior authentication required," Malbear Labs said.
"From the XSP host, the agent recovered the system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three additional private keys with certificate matches confirmed. The system identity key is used by the BroadWorks platform to authenticate between its own components; possessing it allows impersonation of the XSP in inter-component communication."
Since November 2021, CISA has added 103 Cisco vulnerabilities to its list of actively exploited flaws, seven of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs.

AntiFox AI 渗透测试平台与访问 AWS 生产机密的攻击有关
AntiFox AI 渗透测试平台与访问 AWS 生产机密的攻击有关
Ravie Lakshmanan著作2026年11月11日人工智能/网络安全
网络安全研究人员披露了一项活动的详细信息，其中一种名为 AntiFox 的新兴代理渗透测试平台被用来窃取 Amazon Web Services (AWS) 凭证并横向转移到受感染的环境中。
Arctic Wolf Labs 在与 The Hacker News 分享的一份报告中表示：“在最近观察到的几起入侵事件中，托管 AntiFox 接口的阿里云系统与针对面向互联网的 Web 服务和相关 AWS 环境的已确认的恶意行为有关。”
据观察，该活动将 Web 开发和 Web shell 部署链接在一起，以促进配置发现、凭证验证、云服务枚举、秘密访问和存储操作。
AntiFox 可从 GitHub 下载，被描述为人工智能 (AI) 驱动的自主渗透测试平台。截至撰写本文时，该项目已被分叉 251 次，并被加星 474 次。
在其自述文件页面上，项目维护者指出 -
给定授权目标，计划者/工作人员/主代理多代理系统在双图核心（全局资产图+每个任务探索图）上运行全面参与——侦察→攻击面发现→利用→发现捕获→报告交付——完全可观察、交互式和可交付
与大多数“擅长发现，但止步于发现”的自动化渗透测试工具不同，AntiFox 更注重交付——将人工智能发现的内容转化为工程师可以理解、重现、提供证据的报告，然后直接交给客户。
据 Arctic Wolf 称，一些初始访问活动与受损的面向互联网的互联网信息服务 (IIS) 应用程序相关。然后利用该访问权限使用 IIS 工作进程“w3wp.exe”创建 ASPX Web shell，并运行操作系统命令来执行以下操作 -
运行 PowerShell 命令来查找 web.config 文件和配置备份
读取应用程序设置和数据库连接字符串
枚举调试和错误日志目录
尝试使用从应用程序配置中提取的凭据连接到内部生产数据库
将配置和日志文件复制到可通过 Web 访问的上传目录中
Arctic Wolf 表示：“在受感染的 IIS 服务器上，通过 w3wp.exe 运行的命令使用 whoami 识别执行上下文，枚举应用程序目录，使用 icacls 检查权限，并测试将文件写入 Web 根目录的能力。”
“w3wp.exe 创建 ASPX Web shell，然后通过同一 IIS 工作进程执行命令，这表明受影响的 Web 应用程序受到了损害。”
用于在 IIS 服务器上执行代码的具体漏洞尚不清楚。在其他攻击中，据说威胁行为者是从通过尚未确定的方式获得的有效 AWS 凭证开始的。
具体来说，这涉及滥用有效的 IAM 身份来验证凭证并枚举数十种服务，包括 IAM、EC2、S3、Lambda、Secrets Manager、KMS、RDS、ECS、EKS、Redshift、Athena、Glue、Systems Manager、API Gateway、CloudWatch、CloudFormation、DynamoDB 和 Amazon Bedrock。

【原文 English Original】
AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
AntiFox AI Pentesting Platform Linked to Attacks That Accessed AWS Production Secrets
Ravie LakshmananNov 11, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Web Security
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a campaign in which an emerging agentic penetration testing platform called AntiFox has been used to steal Amazon Web Services (AWS) credentials and pivot laterally into compromised environments.
"In several recently observed intrusions, Alibaba Cloud systems hosting AntiFox interfaces were associated with confirmed malicious actions against internet-facing web services and associated AWS environments," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News.
The activity has been observed chaining together web exploitation and web shell deployment to facilitate configuration discovery, credential validation, cloud-service enumeration, secret access, and storage operations.
AntiFox, available for download from GitHub, has been described as an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven autonomous penetration testing platform. As of writing, the project has been forked 251 times and starred 474 times.
On its README page, the project maintainer states -
Given an authorized target, a planner / worker / main-agent multi-agent system runs the full engagement over a dual-graph core (a global asset graph + a per-task exploration graph) — recon → attack-surface discovery → exploitation → finding capture → report delivery — fully observable, interactive, and deliverable
Unlike most automated pentest tools that are "great at discovery, but stop at discovery," AntiFox puts its weight on delivery — turning what the AI finds into a report that an engineer can understand, reproduce, back with evidence, and hand straight to the client.
According to Arctic Wolf, some of the initial access activity is associated with a compromised internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) application. The access is then leveraged to create an ASPX web shell using "w3wp.exe," the IIS worker process, and run operating system commands to perform the following actions -
Run PowerShell commands to locate web.config files and configuration backups
Read application settings and database connection strings
Enumerate debug and error-log directories
Attempts to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from the application configuration
Copy configuration and log files into a web-accessible upload directory
"On a compromised IIS server, commands run through w3wp.exe identified the execution context with whoami, enumerated the application directory, checked permissions with icacls, and tested the ability to write files into the web root," Arctic Wolf said.
"The creation of an ASPX web shell by w3wp.exe, followed by command execution through the same IIS worker process, suggests compromise through the affected web application."
The precise vulnerability used to achieve code execution on the IIS server is not known. In other attacks, the threat actor is said to have started with a valid AWS credential obtained through as-yet-undetermined means.
Specifically, this involved abusing valid IAM identities to validate credentials and enumerate dozens of services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, Redshift, Athena, Glue, Systems Manager, API Gateway, CloudWatch, CloudFormation, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock.
While a majority of these authenticated cross-service API requests ended up with an "AccessDenied" error, some of the discovery and secret-access operations were successful, according to the cybersecurity company.
In at least some instances, the activity has been observed progressing beyond Secrets Manager enumeration to a successful GetSecretValue request against a production secret. Elsewhere, a valid AWS identity was used for S3 discovery and object operations via API calls.
"Agentic frameworks such as these make penetration testing techniques more accessible to threat actors, while increasing the speed and consistency with which these techniques can be applied in live attacks," Arctic Wolf said.
The disclosure comes as threat actors are increasingly weaponizing AI-powered penetration testing tools like ARTEX to conduct broad-scale attacks across the world, enabling them to automate various stages of an intrusion with minimal human intervention.
The integration of AI has allowed adversaries, both large and small, to adapt established tradecraft and deploy them at machine speed, making it possible to progress from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes.
Earlier this week, VECERT disclosed details of a campaign dubbed Operation Ghost-Campus orchestrated by a Chinese threat actor that uses AI agents to maintain perpetual, cost-free access to large language models (LLMs) and eventually perform automated academic fraud and steal data belonging to over 5,000 students enrolled at the Fengxian Campus.
"The agent industrializes the creation of accounts on the search engine fofa.info, scans the global cyberspace for misconfigured servers, extracts API keys for OpenAI and DeepSeek, automatically verifies their financial balances, and injects them into the attacker's development environment," VECERT said.
"This stolen computing power fuels an interactive GoTTY terminal ('Pi — AI Coding Assistant') and, by extension, provides intelligence to the scripts that sustain academic fraud bots ('heartbeat' bots) and extractors of financial data and personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to thousands of students at the Fengxian Campus."
According to data from Censys, there are 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026, with most of them located in the U.S., Hong Kong, China, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea. However, it's worth noting that not every instance is necessarily malicious in nature.
In a separate report, Check Point Research said it identified 2,557 systems that hosted ARTEX, including 10 misconfigured instances exposing their full databases.
"In many observed cases, ARTEX required remarkably little interaction from its operators once an objective had been established," Check Point said. "Rather than continuously directing attacks step by step, operators frequently issued a goal and left the agent fleet to work toward it. Human interactions were largely limited to checking progress, asking whether a target had been compromised or occasionally adjusting priorities."
The vast majority of the attacks are designed to siphon cryptocurrency, steal Apple code-signing certificates, compromise gaming accounts, and conduct denial-of-service (DoS) attacks against gambling websites. The activity has been found to exploit vulnerabilities related to weak or hard-coded passwords, missing authentication, insecure direct object references, and remote code execution.
In the campaign targeting Apple code-signing certificates, ARTEX agents searched compromised systems for certificate databases, followed by validating the stolen certificates by checking passwords, private keys, Apple revocation status, expiration dates, and associated provisioning profiles.
Ultimately, the activity is estimated to have harvested more than 300 certificates and their passwords, out of which three certificates passed the full validation process and could be used to sign arbitrary iOS applications.
The biggest change brought by agentic hacking to the cyber threat landscape is scale and speed, Check Point cautioned, as a cybercriminal with limited technical skills can task AI agents with investigating a number of targets in parallel and exploiting them using known and zero-day vulnerabilities with less manual effort.
"Its relevance to us lies in its scale, speed and persistence," CERT-EU said in an alert. "ARTEX can test large numbers of low-complexity misconfigurations, including those a human tester would notice but not have time to check, and it can work through long attack chains without the fatigue that limits manual testing."
"The same is true of complex payload crafting. Exploitation paths that need carefully tailored payloads often take more effort than the severity of the finding justifies, so a manual assessment may leave them untested."
Tools like AntiFox and ARTEX are part of a broader set of about 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that are engineered to connect to an LLM and can act on outputs autonomously. They fall under five broad categories -
Network kill chain capable of end-to-end reconnaissance, exploitation, and post-exploitation: PentAGI, RedAmon, and DarkMoon
Web-app and API: Strix, Shannon, and PentestGPT
C2-integrated: Sage, echidna, Pojun, and FORANG
Harnesses: RAPTOR, CyberStrike, cyber-harness, Nebula and Cybermes
Research prototypes: Incalmo, hackingBuddyGPT, VulnBot, HackSynth, AutoPT, and Ares
"Each framework has public source code and wires a model into a loop that runs tools and acts on their output," GitGuardian said.
"Agentic AI pentesting tools hand their agent a shell and web access, so the model can assemble a pipeline at runtime. A GitHub search, a scanner download, and a found key passed to the next call are all one prompt away, even though none of it ships in the repository."
